rule: Supported for the described factory-steamed, rolled and dried plain tea by an explicit scope inference. Bahrain's enacted GCC Plant Quarantine Law Article 2 covers living plants and manufactured plant products that can introduce or spread pests; Articles 15(1) and 15(3) address covered consignments and risk-based waivers. ISPM32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify manufactured tea as Category 1. Applied as factual evidence to the domestic definition, the sealed finished sencha falls outside the pest-risk-qualified manufactured-product limb; it does not need an individual waiver to be outside that limb. Article 31(1) requires measures to conform with IPPC/WTO-SPS standards, but is not treated as automatically adopting every ISPM. The current 2024 food guide separately allows regular food without prior registration/authorization and provides a personal-use route with recipient undertaking, suitable personal quantity, Arabic/English labels and possible inspection.
personalMailApplicability: The conclusion uses the generally applicable domestic product definition and the food guide's non-commercial-import section, not a traveller-only concession. Japan MAFF's postal PQ*11 entry preserves a processing exception; its default is not treated as proof that manufactured Category 1 tea is covered. Ordinary postal Customs declarations and recipient food-clearance declarations remain required.
authority: Destination agricultural/food authority; Japan MAFF Plant Protection Station where cited
researchAttempts: Read Bahrain NPPO phytosanitary notice and 2026 ministry service including traveller-only exemption.

A routine recipient undertaking is not itself an official certificate. The unresolved agricultural classification under the MAFF PQ*11 processing exception still prevents clearance.

30 September bounded independent processing/list peer review: downloaded the complete 23-page English Plant Quarantine Law submitted by Bahrain NPPO to IPPC, OCRed the image PDF, and visually checked PDF pages 7 and 9. Article 2 defines manufactured products by pest risk. Article 15(1) supplies permit/certificate defaults; 15(3) authorises commodity risk-based waivers but grants no enumerated automatic processing waiver. Article 24 addresses goods in travellers’ possession and cannot be extended to post. The annex on PDF pp.12–23 is Bahrain’s regulated-pest lists, not an exhaustive list of controlled/exempt food commodities; absence of tea there therefore proves nothing about its category. No outcome change. Source PDF/OCR saved in middle-east-definition-peer-review/.

This is a regulatory compatibility duty, not express automatic domestic adoption of ISPM32 Category1. Reassessed the precise Article2 living-plants/manufactured-product boundary against the actual ISPM32 Appendix2 Tea example (visually verified by the root audit); Article15(3) individual waiver is not logically required for goods outside the definition. Article31 supports standards-consistent interpretation but is not used as an automatic treaty exemption. This supersedes the earlier assumption that absence of a named tea ruling necessarily leaves processing scope unresolved.

Verified current Bahrain government service explicitly cites national Law5/2003 adopting the GCC quarantine law, plus Decision1/2004; recovered national enacting text from FAO for provenance. No absence of a tariff restriction cell or generic international membership was used as an exemption.
permitFreeReason: Explicit legal-scope and manufacturing inference: the operative national law limits manufactured plant products by pest risk, and the actual ISPM32 tea example supports the finding that factory-made, sealed steamed/rolled/dried sencha is outside that class. A missing Customs agency lookup does not require a bespoke ruling where this general definition suffices. Use the separate official personal-food route, supply Arabic or English product labelling, and have the recipient complete the routine personal-use undertaking if requested. This is not a claim of a tea-specific Bahrain ruling or an exemption for raw dried herbs, seeds, blends or contaminated goods.
requiredDocument: Ordinary postal/Customs declaration; recipient written personal-use undertaking for food clearance; Arabic or English label. If only another language is supplied, the guide requires an approved translation-office sticker, so use an adequate English/Arabic label initially to stay within the no-special-documents constraint.
finding: New complete official English personal-food guide recovered; independently applied the already-recovered domestic manufactured-product definition to the actual ISPM32 manufactured-tea example. This closes the no-special-documents route by an explicitly labelled scope/manufacturing inference.
customsCommodityReview: Government-notified tariff agency lookup remains inaccessible, and blank tariff procedure cells were not treated as proof of clearance. The supported outcome instead follows the operative risk-qualified product definition and independently verified manufactured-tea evidence.
foodImportReview: Complete current OFOQ English Food Importers Guide (updated April 2024) recovered successfully. Printed p5 item3(b) says regular food needs no prior registration or authorization; pp17–18 separately prescribe a personal-use undertaking, quantity within the allowance, Arabic/English labels (or approved translation), lawful ingredients and possible laboratory inspection. Commercial company registration and origin health-certificate procedures elsewhere in the guide are not automatically transferred into this separate personal section. The guide gives no numerical personal tea maximum; this finding is limited to a single 100 g package as an ordinary personal-use amount, not an unlimited or invented statutory allowance.
inferenceLevel: Domestic legal-scope and commodity-manufacturing inference; no tea-specific national ruling.
conditions: Only plain factory-manufactured Camellia sinensis tea, steamed/rolled/dried and sealed; not raw dried leaves/herbs, planting material, blends or infested goods.
One 100 g package for genuine recipient personal consumption, with no resale/distribution; this is the assessed quantity, not a verified statutory maximum.
Arabic or English product label and routine personal-use undertaking; ordinary Customs/arrival inspection and any lawful charges apply.
